questions.question: A coding model proposes a faster algorithm but cannot reliably tell whether its own claim is true. What closes that loop?
options: Select the newest candidate without comparing its behavior
Ask the same model to describe its code more confidently
Keep only candidates with the shortest source files
Run a machine-checkable evaluator on each candidate
questions.explanation: Each proposed variant needs an external, machine-checkable test or benchmark that evaluates behavior rather than the model’s description of it. Confident self-report or short source code is not evidence that the program works.

questions.question: In the AlphaEvolve loop, what happens after a candidate is produced?
options: Compile, run, score, then archive it if useful
Publish it immediately and ask users for feedback
Train the evaluator to accept its reported score
Replace every parent before checking the candidate
questions.explanation: Compile and run a candidate, score its behavior, then add it to the archive only if it is useful. Publishing before evaluation can promote broken code; the model-reported score is not a substitute for the evaluator.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a MAP-elites-style archive in the lesson?
options: Replace the evaluator with a diversity score
Store only the single highest-scoring program
Remove every candidate that differs from the current leader
Keep strong candidates across different feature-vector cells
questions.explanation: MAP-elites stores strong candidates by feature-vector cell, preserving alternatives across search regions. Keeping only one global winner can collapse exploration, and a diversity score alone cannot replace correctness evaluation.

questions.question: An optimizer removes comments and passes the measured code-quality proxy without changing behavior. What failure does this illustrate?
options: A reduction in search diversity caused by MAP-elites
Reward hacking against an imperfect evaluator
A failure of parallel call correlation
A correct held-out improvement in task performance
questions.explanation: Reward hacking is improving the measured proxy without improving intended behavior. Removing comments to score a code-quality proxy exploits its definition; it is not a task-performance gain validated on held-out behavior.

questions.question: A candidate looks strong on training inputs. What evaluator design best checks whether it memorized those inputs?
options: Use held-out inputs the candidate generator has not seen
Let the candidate report its own accuracy estimate
Remove correctness checks and compare code length
Score only on the same examples used to propose edits
questions.explanation: Held-out inputs test generalization beyond examples that guided search; scoring on the same inputs can be memorized or overfit. A candidate’s self-estimated accuracy is not independent evaluation.

questions.question: A domain has no fast, deterministic way to score proposed improvements, and every candidate needs expert review. What does the lesson imply?
options: The evaluator can be skipped once the archive is diverse
The AlphaEvolve loop is a poor fit because evaluation is costly
The LLM should replace the missing correctness criterion
The loop is ideal because human judgment is always deterministic
questions.explanation: The loop depends on a rigorous evaluator; if every proposal needs expert review, human judgment becomes the search bottleneck and may be ambiguous. The LLM cannot replace the correctness criterion the domain lacks.
